_comment: Endpoints served at GET /events/<name>?after_event=<id>&limit=<n>.
Every event is stored. An endpoint is a read-side projection: which
categories it serves and which fields it returns. The reduction happens on
the collector, so a reader that wants one category, with a few fields,
transfers far less than the whole store. A field an event has no value for
is left out of the response rather than written as null.
`all` below serves everything. To serve a subset, add an endpoint of your
own - for example:
"moves": {
"categories": ["move"],
"fields": ["event", "time", "actor", "origin", "destination"]
Omit `categories` to serve every category, and `fields` to serve every
column. Nothing listed here decides what is kept: the store holds every
category either way, so an endpoint can be added or changed without losing
anything.
This file is mounted into the query service, not baked into how it works.
Edit it and restart that one container; nothing needs rebuilding.
A category listed here that the store holds nothing for yields an empty
result, and the service says so on startup rather than leaving you to
wonder whether none have happened.
max_rows caps one response. Clients page with after_event=<highest event
received>, which is exclusive, so a row is never returned twice. The
x-akiraka-last-event header carries that cursor, so a client need not parse
the body to find it.
Set AKIRAKA_QUERY_TOKEN to require a bearer token on every request but
/health. Do that before binding anywhere but loopback.
Delete this file to fall back to the built-in `all` endpoint.

all._comment: The whole store, in event-id order. Categories are omitted so every one is served. The bulky `data` field is not served here: the event columns are what a reader needs to keep its own copy current, and `data` is much the largest thing in the store. max_rows is high because that is the point of this endpoint - a full catch-up at the 10000 default would be thousands of requests.
